Grande Acedrex is documented in the *Libro de los Juegos* by Alfonso X of Castile, c. 1283. Rules from chessvariants.com/historic.dir/acedrex.html (Hans Bodlaender, from Murray, Gollon, and Pritchard).

Designed by Gary Gygax. Published in *Dragon Magazine* No. 100 (TSR Inc., August 1985), pages 34–40. Game rules are not subject to copyright. \n \n Authoritative secondary source: Edward Jackman with Hans Bodlaender, *Dragonchess*, chessvariants.com (1995–1996), which addresses ambiguities in Gygax's original description. This rulebook follows chessvariants.com where it conflicts with later re-descriptions, including a naming correction for Hero, Thief, Cleric, and Paladin relative to the Wikipedia article on Dragonchess.

Hexapawn was invented by Martin Gardner, published in *Scientific American*, March 1962 (reprinted in *The Unexpected Hanging and Other Mathematical Diversions*). Chessvariants.com page written by Robert Price.
Hole Chess was created by Gary K. Gifford, December 2003. Entry in the Chess Variants 44-Square Contest. Source: chessvariants.com/44.dir/hole-chess.html

Metamachy was designed by Jean-Louis Cazaux (France, 2012). Rules sourced from The Chess Variant Pages at chessvariants.com/rules/metamachy.
Nightrider piece invented by T. R. Dawson, 1925. Public domain. Rules in the public domain. Implemented in Fairy-Stockfish, Green Chess, and Zillions of Games.
Oblong Chess is a historical Shatranj variant approximately one thousand years old. Written by Hans Bodlaender. Source: chessvariants.com/historic.dir/oblong.html (created November 1995).

Halma. Invented 1883, George Howard Monks, Boston. Public domain. Rules confirmed from Ludeme/Ludii (Maastricht University game research library) and Atvriders/cards-and-such halma-quiz (independent rules confirmation). Piece count independently confirmed by jeromydarling/heritage-parlor.

Prosperity. Published by the Adgame Company (Inc.), Washington, D.C., 1932. Designed by Elizabeth Magie Phillips. US Patent 1,509,312 (filed 1923, granted 1924). Public domain (patent expired 1941). Aviation. Published by H.P. Gibson & Sons Ltd., London. Part of the Gibson hidden-rank warfare series alongside L’Attaque, Dover Patrol, and Tri-Tactics. Gibson Aviation rulebook (scanned from physical copy, 2004 digitisation).

L'Attaque. Designed by Hermance Edan. French patent No. 396,795 filed 26 November 1908. First published 1910 by Au Jeu Retrouvé, France. Rights acquired 1925 by H.P. Gibson & Sons, London. Public domain rule set. Gibson & Sons revised-edition rulebook (scanned from physical copy) and Value Table card.
Bao. Traditional game, Tanzania and East Africa. Public domain. Sources: de Voogt, Alex — *Mancala Board Games* (1997); Wikipedia (CC-BY-SA).

Traditional variant. Public domain. Rules documented in Parlett, D. (1999) *The Oxford History of Board Games*, p. 252. Sources: Ludeme/Ludii — Damenspiel.lud (SHA 47b7ccc6, Maastricht University Ludii Project); Checkers & Draughts Wiki — Deutsches Damespiel article.
Dameo. Invented by Christian Freeling (2000). Rules in the public domain; game rules are not subject to copyright. Source: Wikipedia — Dameo article (CC-BY-SA 4.0).
C. S. Elliott, 1971. Named after Benedict Arnold. Public domain rules.
English Draughts. Public domain. Rules standardised by the World Draughts Federation (FMJD) and the English Draughts Association.
Invented by Dr. G. Arthur Lutze (1813–1870). Documented by Theodor Müller-Alfeld and Heinz Machatscheck. Rules documented from chessvariants.com/multiplayer.dir/vierschach.html (Jörg Knappen, 2002).
Traditional variant. Public domain. Governed by the Federazione Italiana Dama (FID). Source: Wikipedia (CC-BY-SA).
Traditional variant. Public domain. Governed by the Russian Draughts Federation. Source: Wikipedia (CC-BY-SA).
Traditional game originating in China approximately 4,000 years ago. Known as Weiqi (Chinese), Baduk (Korean), Igo (Japanese). Public domain. Rules standardised by the International Go Federation.
Ralph Betza, 1970s–80s. Published in *NOST-algia* newsletter. Public domain.
Traditional variant. Public domain. Governed by the Confederação Brasileira de Jogo de Damas. Source: Wikipedia (CC-BY-SA).
Historical Japanese game, medieval period. Rules documented from chessvariants.com/rules/dai-shogi (H. G. Muller, 2015).
Abdul Jabbar Karwatkar, 1979. Named after his home city of Madras (now Chennai), India. Public domain rules.
Competitive variant of Gomoku. Rules governed by the Renju International Federation. Public domain. The Renju International Federation was founded in Stockholm, Sweden on August 8, 1988.
Kalah. Designed by William Julius Champion Jr., USA, 1940s. Public domain rules. Source: Wikipedia (CC-BY-SA).
Ayo. Traditional game, Yoruba people, Nigeria. Public domain. Source: Wikipedia (CC-BY-SA); Russ, Laurence — *The Complete Mancala Games Book* (1984).
Reversi. Public domain. Invented by Lewis Waterman and John Mollett, England, c. 1883.
Xiangqi 42 was invented by Robert Price as an entry in the Chess Variant Pages 42-squares contest. WWW page created October 17, 2001. Rules documented from chessvariants.com/42.dir/xiangqi42.html.
Jens Bæk Nielsen and Torben Osted, 1989. Popularised on Chess.com. Public domain rules.
Walter Stead, 1953. Published in fairy chess circles. Public domain.
Modern variant. Distinguished from Fog of War by its stricter visibility rules. Public domain.
Traditional game. Public domain. Documented in Libro de los Juegos (Alfonso X, 1283). Source: Wikipedia (CC-BY-SA), Murray's A History of Board Games Other Than Chess (1952).
Ancient origins (11th–14th century Europe, earlier roots in India/Burma). Modern codification by Anne Sunnucks, *The Encyclopaedia of Chess*, 1970. Public domain.
Dragon Chess was created by Grandmaster Miguel Illescas. Rules documented from pychess.org/variants/dragon.
Traditional variant. Public domain. Rules standardised by the World Draughts Federation (FMJD). Source: FMJD Official Rules, Wikipedia (CC-BY-SA).
Tori Shogi was invented by Toyota Genryu (1799). Public domain. Rules documented from pychess.org/variants/torishogi.
Oware. Traditional game, Ghana and West Africa. Public domain. Source: Wikipedia (CC-BY-SA); Russ, Laurence — *The Complete Mancala Games Book* (1984).
Pallanguzhi. Traditional game, Tamil Nadu, India. Public domain. Source: Wikipedia (CC-BY-SA); Russ, Laurence — *The Complete Mancala Games Book* (1984).
Dobutsu Shogi was invented by Madoka Kitao (北尾まどか). Public domain. Rules documented from pychess.org/variants/dobutsu.
Congkak. Traditional game, Malay Archipelago. Public domain. Source: Wikipedia (CC-BY-SA); Russ, Laurence — *The Complete Mancala Games Book* (1984).

Japanese competitive game. Organised by the Ninuki Renju Sha, Japan, 1923-1940. Direct historical precursor to Pente (1977). Public domain. Sources: Renju International Federation (renju.se); Wikipedia (Pente article, Gomoku article).
Traditional variant from Friesland, Netherlands. Public domain. Recognised by the World Draughts Federation (FMJD). Source: Wikipedia (CC-BY-SA).
Sungka. Traditional game, Philippines. Public domain. Source: Wikipedia (CC-BY-SA); Russ, Laurence — *The Complete Mancala Games Book* (1984).
Traditional Russian variant. Public domain. Pre-dates Lasca (1911). Source: Wikipedia (CC-BY-SA).

Described in *The Encyclopedia of Chess Variants* by David Pritchard (1994). Also known as Cannibal Chess (though that name more properly refers to the replacement variant where capturing substitutes movement rather than adding it). Public domain.

Yalta Chess documented by Daniel Lindström; WWW page by David Howe, created May 12, 1997. Rules and board graphic documented from chessvariants.com/multiplayer.dir/yalta.html. Board shape (hexagonal Y-trisection, not circular), player colours, and back-rank order confirmed against the primary source's diagrams, 2026-07.
Invented by Emanuel Lasker (World Chess Champion), 1911. Public domain. Source: Wikipedia + Lasker 1911 (CC-BY-SA).

Single Tax. Rules from the Economic Game Company edition, New York, 1906. Designed by Elizabeth J. Magie. Public domain. Sources: landlordsgame.info/rules/lg-1906_rulebook.html (transcription via hoelzl/L3 public repository); Wikipedia: The Landlord's Game (CC-BY-SA).

1906 Commercial Edition. Rules from the Economic Game Company edition, New York, 1906. Designed by Elizabeth J. Magie. Public domain. Source: landlordsgame.info/rules/lg-1906_rulebook.html (transcription via hoelzl/L3 public repository).

1904 Original. Rules from US Patent 748,626, granted January 5, 1904. Designed by Elizabeth J. Magie. Public domain (patent expired 1921). Sources: US Patent 748,626 (public domain); hoelzl/L3 GitHub repository patent transcription, sourced from landlordsgame.info.
Origins in 6th-century India (Chaturanga). Modern rules standardised by FIDE. Public domain.
